prompt: Which protocol stroke uses HTTP/3?

options.text: HTTP/3 over TCP over UDP
HTTP/3 over QIC over UDP
HTTP/3 over TLS over TCP
HTTP/3 directly over Ethernet without IP

explanation: HTTP/3 uses QUIC as transport. QUIC runs over UDP and handles, among other things, reliable transmission, flows and integrated security.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF pages 27, 70, 75–76

prompt: What is the main idea of multiplexing in HTTP/2?

options.text: Frames from multiple HTTP streams can be interleaved on one connection.
Every HTTP request must have its own TCP connection.
All responses are merged into one document without a stream identifier.
TCP delivers packets with no ordering requirement.

explanation: HTTP/2 splits messages into frames identified by stream ID. It can interleave the frames, and the receiver can reassemble each stream.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF pages 52, 55

prompt: The statelessness of HTTP prevents a network application from using cookies to keep track of a logged-in user.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Statelessness describes the HTTP request-answer model. However, the application may link requests to a session using, for example, cookies.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF page 16

prompt: How does a HTTP/2 receiver know which stream a frame belongs to?

options.text: The flows are only identified by the arrival order.
The TCP sequence number is identical to the HTTP stream number.
The frame contains a stream identifier.
Each stream always uses its own destination port.

explanation: The HTTP/2 framework has a stream ID. One TCP connection can therefore support multiple logical streams.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF pages 52, 55

prompt: HTTP/2's binary inclusion in itself means that GET and POST get quite different meanings from HTTP/1.1.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Keep the HTTP Semantics. The binary inclusion changes how messages are encoded and transmitted, not the meaning of the methods.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF page 49

prompt: Three requests have been sent with HTTP/1.1 pipelining. The first answer is slow to produce. Why can later answers be delayed even if they are ready?

options.text: The responses must be sent in the order of the requests without merging the response content.
Pipelining allows only one outstanding request.
HTTP/1.1 must wait until all replies have been completed before the first one is sent.
Each pipeline request requires a new TCP connection.

explanation: Pipelining allows the client to send multiple requests, but the HTTP/1.1 responses need to continue to be serialised in the correct order. An early response can therefore block subsequent responses at application level.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF pages 39, 41

prompt: A HTTP/2 connection carries streams A and B. A TCP segment with data from A is lost, while later TCP segments with B arrive. What could happen?

options.text: B is always delivered immediately because HTTP/2 does not use TCP.
Only HTTP headers are lost; data do not need retransmission.
B needs to create a new IP address to continue.
TCP can hold back later byte also for B until the hole in the ordered byte stream is repaired.

explanation: HTTP/2 removes the application restriction from merging responses, but TCP exposes one ordered byte stream. Thus, losses can lead to head-of-line blocking across HTTP/2 streams.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF pages 55, 68

prompt: In QUIC lost bytes can still delay later bytes in the same reliable, ordered stream.

options.text: True
False

explanation: QUIC separates the supply of flows from each other, but a single reliable flow has still ordered delivery. The advantage is that a hole by itself does not have to block delivery on other flows.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF page 75

prompt: What description distinguishes correctly between flow control and congestion control in QUIC?

options.text: Separate flows mean that network loading can never affect multiple flows simultaneously.
Flow control protects recipient capacity; congestion control adapts transmission to network capacity.
Flow control encrypts data; congestion control selects HTTP method.
Both just means UDP has a fixed maximum package speed.

explanation: QUIC applies flow control to the data a receiver can accept, including per-stream limits, and congestion control to the transport connection. Independent stream delivery does not give streams independent capacity at a shared bottleneck.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF page 75

prompt: What uses HTTP/2 header compression to reduce repeated transmission?

options.text: Sender and Receiver can use indexes to header values they already know.
TCP sequence numbers automatically replace all HTTP headers.
HTTP/2 only compresses response content, while headers always repeat unchanged.
Repeated headers are sent on a separate connection outside HTTP/2.

explanation: An indexed collection of header fields allows repeated values to be referenced to compact. This is particularly useful when many requests have similar heads.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF page 64

prompt: The connection ID of a QUIC connection can help to continue the connection when changing the client's IP address.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Connection ID reduces identity dependence on the normal IP/port combination. It provides support for interconnection; the new path must continue to be managed and validated by the protocol.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF page 80

prompt: What statement about starting QUIC best fits the lecture model?

options.text: QUIC first requires a separate TCP handshake and then two UDP handshake.
TLS is not relevant since QUIC is using UDP.
A new connection may use \(1\,\mathrm{RTT}\), while the resumption of a previous connection may allow 0-RTT data.
All clients can always send secure 0-RTT data without prior contact.

explanation: QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 into startup. 0-RTT is an option for recovery with previously established state, not a universal property of a completely new connection.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF pages 76, 78–79

prompt: Use the HTTP/1.0 model from the lecture: \(1\,\mathrm{RTT}\) for TCP configuration, \(1\,\mathrm{RTT}\) from HTTP request to first answer change, then object transfer. RTT is \(40\,\mathrm{ms}\) and the object takes \(20\,\mathrm{ms}\) to transfer. Ignore DNS, TLS and server work. What's the total going to be?

options.text: \(140\,\mathrm{ms}\)
\(100\,\mathrm{ms}\)
\(60\,\mathrm{ms}\)
\(80\,\mathrm{ms}\)

explanation: The total is \(2\times\mathrm{RTT}+\text{transmission time}=2\times40\,\mathrm{ms}+20\,\mathrm{ms}=100\,\mathrm{ms}\). Add the transmission time to the two round-trip times.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF page 32

prompt: Six objects are fetched sequentially. Assume \(1\,\mathrm{RTT}\) for each TCP configuration and \(1\,\mathrm{RTT}\) per request response, ignore transfer time, DNS and TLS. How much time does one reused TCP connection save compared to a new connection per object when \(\mathrm{RTT}=30\,\mathrm{ms}\)?

options.text: \(150\,\mathrm{ms}\)
\(30\,\mathrm{ms}\)
\(180\,\mathrm{ms}\)
\(330\,\mathrm{ms}\)

explanation: Six new connections cost \(6\times(1+1)\,\mathrm{RTT}=12\,\mathrm{RTT}\). One reuse cost \(1+6=7\,\mathrm{RTT}\). The difference is \(5\,\mathrm{RTT}=150\,\mathrm{ms}\). This applies to the explicit sequential model without pipelining.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF pages 32, 36

prompt: Two independent documents are fetched on streams A and B. Some data from A is lost, and all required data from B has arrived. What is the most precise difference between HTTP/2 over TCP and HTTP/3 over QUIC?

options.text: HTTP/3 must retransmit both documents while HTTP/2 never retransmits.
HTTP/2 has an independent TCP byte stream per HTTP stream on the same connection.
QUIC guarantees that B is not affected by shared congestion or capacity.
TCP can block delivery of B behind a gap. QUIC can deliver B independently if B itself has no missing data.

explanation: TCP delivers an ordered byte stream and can therefore hold back B. QUIC orders delivery per stream, so bytes already received on B need not wait for A. Shared congestion control and capacity can still affect subsequent transmission.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF pages 68, 75

prompt: A QUIC packet with packet number 42 will be lost. The data must be re-dispatched. What is correct according to the description of package numbers in the lecture?

options.text: All subsequent packets must use 42 until it is confirmed.
Package numbers are only used during start-up, not for re-transmission.
The data is sent in a new packet with a new packet number.
Package number 42 needs to be reused in order to recognise the data.

explanation: QUIC does not re-use package numbers for retransmission. The identity of the change of content in the stream is different from the package number of the transfer that carries them.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF page 80

prompt: An app has 20 independent small answers and a very large response to one connection. What change allows small answers to be merged while the large answer is still being transferred, without a connection per answer?

options.text: Switching all requests from GET to POST.
Switching from HTTP/1.1 response serialisation to HTTP/2 frameworks and streams.
Increase the number of HTTP/1.1 queries in the pipeline, without other changes.
Remove stream ID from the HTTP/2 frames.

explanation: The HTTP/2 framework can be distributed between flows during the transfer. HTTP/1.1 pipelining sends multiple requests, but does not cancel the requirement for serialised responses.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF pages 39, 41, 52, 55

prompt: A receiver has little buffer space for current A, but plenty for current B. Why is flow control per stream useful, even if both use the same QUIC connection?

options.text: The receiver may limit A without exactly A's buffer limit having to stop B.
This guarantees that B always gets the whole width of the link.
It eliminates the need for congestion control for the connection.
This means that lost bytes on A can be delivered in any order.

explanation: Per-stream control allows the receiver to control the consumption of each current. Other limits, such as the overall flow control of the link and the capacity of the network, may continue to restrict both.
source: HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC · PDF page 75

prompt: What is the characteristic of cloud calculation in the definition used in the lecture?

options.text: A fixed allocation of physical servers that can only be changed by re-buying.
That the customer must own the infrastructure and manually install each service.
Remote storage on its own, without the possibility of offering processing or other facilities.
Access, where necessary, to a shared pool of resources that can be quickly clarified and released.

explanation: This definition focuses on network access where necessary, shared configurable resources and rapid preparation and release with restricted administration.

prompt: A customer leases virtual machines and selects and maintains itself operating systems and applications. Which service model is this?

options.text: SaaS
Community cloud
IaaS
PaaS

explanation: IaaS provides basic processing, storage and networks. The customer controls guest operating systems and applications; the supplier handles the underlying infrastructure. Community cloud is a distribution model, not the same axis.

prompt: A developer uploads his or her own application to the provider's driving environment, but does not manage the operating system. What's best for you?

options.text: A physically dedicated server without cloud services
PaaS
IaaS with full OS administration
SaaS where the supplier delivers the full end-user application

explanation: PaaS lets the customer develop and run its own applications on the supplier's platform. The customer has control over the application, but not the entire infrastructure and operating system.

prompt: A private cloud must always be physically located in the organisation's own building according to the definition of the lecture.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Private means that the infrastructure is for one organisation. It may be operated by a third party and located either with the organisation or externally.

prompt: What alternative is an example of SaaS?

options.text: A rented virtual machine where the customer installs the operating system.
An empty physical server the customer buys and puts in his own rack.
A platform where the customer’s main responsibility is to deliver its own application code.
A complete online application using and configuring functions without managing the operating system.

explanation: SaaS provides the application as a service. The customer uses the features and may have limited configuration options, while the supplier operates applications and underlying resources.

prompt: What does elasticity distinguish from just having large capacity?

options.text: Elasticity means that a fixed server park is always the maximum dimension.
Elasticity means only moving unchanged capacity to another supplier.
The amount of resources can grow and shrink with the need.
Elasticity means that capacity can be increased but never reduced.

explanation: Elasticity is about adapting allocated resources to demand. A large fixed server park can have high capacity without being elastic.

prompt: Multitenancy removes the need for isolation between customer data because everyone uses the same application.

options.text: True
False

explanation: When several organisations share an application, the isolation of data and configuration is particularly important. Resource sharing does not mean that customers should be able to read each other's data.

prompt: An establishment retains a private cloud and connects it to a public cloud so that the load can be moved between them. Which distribution model best fits?

options.text: Hybrid cloud
Community cloud only because two environments exist
SaaS
One public cloud without a private part

explanation: A hybrid cloud combines specific cloud environments with technologies that allow interaction and portability. Service models that SaaS describes a different dimension.

prompt: Which point best fits as a measurable part of an SLA?

options.text: That the supplier promises that the service is "magnificent modern".
That all customers think the interface is nice.
That the service uses the word cloud in the product name.
Contracted availability for a measurement period and how to deal with breaches.

explanation: A SLA concretes the level of service, such as availability, response time or throughput, as well as the follow-up of breaches. Marketing words alone do not give measurable obligations.

prompt: The presentation of multiple virtual machines on one physical machine is an example of the multiplication of resources.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Multiplexing provides more logical resources from one physical resource. Aggregation goes the opposite way by presenting more physical resources as one logical resource.

prompt: Load balancing can distribute requests between servers, but a load balancing device without a rounding can be a single error point.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Redundant application servers are not sufficient if all traffic has to pass through one component that could fail. The architecture must be assessed to the end.

prompt: A SLA promises \(99.9\,\%\) accessibility for a period of exactly 30 days. Assume that all downtime counts equally. How much downtime does the limit equal?

options.text: 43.2 minutes
4.32 minutes
432 minutes
0.432 minutes

explanation: \(30 \times  24 \times  60 = 43\,200\) minutes. The allowed proportion downtime is \(1 - 0.999 = 0.001\). This makes \(43\,200 \times  0.001 = 43.2\) minutes. Otherwise, the actual measurement rules of the contract must be specified.

prompt: Four identical servers each handle a maximum of 200 requests/s. The system shall withstand one server falling out without exceeding this limit. Assume the ideal distribution of cargo and no other bottleneck. What is the maximum sustained load that meets the requirement?

options.text: 800 requests/s
200 requests/s
1,000 requests/s
600 requests/s

explanation: On one error, three servers are left. \(3 \times  200 = 600\) requests/s are therefore the limit. The normal total capacity of 800 is not the same as capacity under the design error.

prompt: A test service requires four instances of 6 hours and one instance of the remaining 18 hours per day. Each service hour costs 2 kr; disregard other costs. How much does elastic adjustment per day save against driving four instances a day?

options.text: 48 kr
192 kr
108 kr
84 kr

explanation: Fixed operation uses \(4 \times  24 = 96\) instance hours and costs 192 kr. Custom operation uses \(4 \times  6 + 1 \times  18 = 42\) instance hours and costs 84 kr. The saving is \(192 - 84 = 108\,\mathrm{kr}\).

prompt: A host has 16 CPU kernels and \(24\,\mathrm{GiB}\) memory. 4 kernels and \(8\,\mathrm{GiB}\) are reserved for the host system. Each VM requires 4 dedicated kernels and \(6\,\mathrm{GiB}\) memory; overbooking is not allowed. Ignore other limitations. How many such VMs can fit at the same time?
explanation: For VMs, 12 cores and \(16\,\mathrm{GiB}\) remain. The CPUs provide space for \(\frac{12}{4} = 3\) VMs, but the memory only gives \(\left\lfloor\frac{16}{6}\right\rfloor=2\). Both resource requirements have to be met, so memory limits to 2.

prompt: Three research institutions will share cloud infrastructure with common requirements for safety, governance and access. The infrastructure is for this community, not the public. Which model describes this most precisely?

options.text: Community cloud
Public cloud because more than one organisation uses it
Hybrid cloud only because three organisations participate
IaaS irrespective of what services are provided

explanation: Community cloud is targeted at several organisations with common concerns and requirements. Hybrid requires a combination of special clouds, while IaaS denotes the level of service and not the nature of the cloud.

prompt: What is the role of a PE route in the MPLS network shown in the lecture?

options.text: It is the customer's edge panes, which are described in the model CE.
It is a clean core route with no responsibility for customer services.
It is the label distribution protocol that is run between routers.
It is at the edge of the supplier network and connects the customer page to the MPLS services.

explanation: PE means Provider Edge. CE is Customer Edge on the customer side, while P denotes a core unit in the supplier network.

prompt: What does the MPLS operation swap mean?

options.text: To remove the outer label without replacing it.
To remove the entire label stack and just treat the IP header.
To replace an incoming label with an outgoing label.
To place a new label in front of the existing stack.

explanation: Label switching uses operations like push, swap and pop. Swap swaps the label used for forwarding on the path.

prompt: How big is one MPLS label stack entry, with all the fields included?

options.text: \(40\,\mathrm{bit}\)
\(32\,\mathrm{bit}\)
\(20\,\mathrm{bit}\)
\(24\,\mathrm{bit}\)

explanation: The label value uses \(20\,\mathrm{bit}\) but the whole entry also contains \(3\,\mathrm{bit}\) TC/EXP, \(1\,\mathrm{bit}\) S and \(8\,\mathrm{bit}\) TTL. The sum is \(32\,\mathrm{bit}\), which is \(4\,\mathrm{byte}\).

prompt: What does the S-bit tell you in an MPLS label stack entry?

options.text: Whether the entry is at the bottom of the label stack.
Whether the packet uses TCP or UDP.
Whether the whole packet is encrypted.
Whether or not the router is a CE or PE route.

explanation: S is the bottom-of-stick indicator. It makes it possible to identify the last label entry before the encapsulated payload.

prompt: An FEC groups packets to receive the same forward processing in the MPLS context.

options.text: True
False

explanation: FEC means Forwarding Equipment Class. At the entrance, packets may be classified to such a class and assigned a label or label-switched path.

prompt: What is the role of the LDP in the MPLS configuration presented?

options.text: Authentication of web browsers for web servers.
To guarantee that all label paths are encrypted.
To distribute tag bindings between routers.
To replace all IGP protocols with a new IP address plan.

explanation: LDP is Label Distribution Protocol. In the described basic model, the label distribution interacts with the routine of IGP; MPLS may also use other control plan mechanisms.

prompt: What is the correct distinction between control plan and forwarding plan in MPLS?

options.text: The control plane is used only in CE routers; P- and PE routers have only a forward-sending plan.
The control plane establishes information about paths and tag bindings; the forward plane uses it on packets.
The control plane carries out push and swaps on data packets; the forwarding plane distributes the label bindings.
The forward plane must establish a new LSP for each data packet before it can be sent.

explanation: The control plane distributes and builds conditions. For example, the forwarding planet performs lookups, push, swap and pop based on this condition.

prompt: In an MPLS-VPN with two label levels, the core can be forwarded after the outer label while the internal label identifies a service at the end-point.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The outer label can direct traffic to the correct PE. For example, the internal label distinguishes the VPN or pseudowire context on the receiving PE.

prompt: Two customers both use the 10.0.0.0/24 prefix. What is the purpose of a Route Distinguisher in the VPNv4 routes?

options.text: To force one of the customers to stop using private addresses.
Encrypting the IP prefix so PE cannot read it.
Increasing the TTL for all packets to 255.
To make the boxes unique by combining RD with the IP prefix.

explanation: An RD on \(8\,\mathrm{byte}\) is combined with the IP prefix so that otherwise similar prefixes can be distinguished in the VPN grid distribution. The prefix itself inside the customer does not need to change.

prompt: What statement describes the difference between L3VPN and L2VPN in the lecture model?

options.text: L2VPN means that CE can never use a routing protocol.
L3VPN and L2VPN distinguish only on the length of the mains line.
At L3VPN, CE shall be routed to PE; at L2VPN CE routes may form routing navels over the service with each other.
L3VPN can only transport Ethernet without IP, while L2VPN must always replace customer routing.

explanation: L3VPN makes the supplier edge involved in the customer's layer 3 routine. L2VPN presents a layer 2 connection, and the customer can place its own layer 3 routine over it.

prompt: A client needs one virtual point-to-point connection between two locations. Which MPLS L2VPN service best suits these?

options.text: Normal IP routine without a layer 2 service
VPWS
VPLS as multi-site virtual LAN
L3VPN where the supplier participates in the customer's IP routine

explanation: VPWS is the point-to-point-oriented service. VPLS models a LAN service that can connect several locations.

prompt: MPLS Fast Reroute always guarantees exactly \(50\,\mathrm{ms}\) recovery, regardless of configuration and type of error.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The lecture uses approximately \(50\,\mathrm{ms}\) as an example of rapid local recovery with prepared spare paths. It is not a universal guarantee regardless of fault detection and configuration.

prompt: A packet is \(1\,500\,\mathrm{byte}\) before MPLS enclosure. Two label entries are added. Ignore layer 2 heads and other plugins. How large is the encapsulated packet?

options.text: \(1\,504\,\mathrm{byte}\)
\(1\,520\,\mathrm{byte}\)
\(1\,564\,\mathrm{byte}\)
\(1\,508\,\mathrm{byte}\)

explanation: One label entry is \(32\,\mathrm{bit} = 4\,\mathrm{byte}\). Two entries add \(8\,\mathrm{byte}\), so \(1\,500 + 8 = 1\,508\,\mathrm{byte}\). The MTU of the transport must take this into account.

prompt: A link allows \(1\,500\,\mathrm{byte}\) for the encapsulated packet, including three MPLS label entries, but without layers of 2 header. How much can the original packet be maximum without exceeding the limit?

options.text: \(1\,480\,\mathrm{byte}\)
\(1\,500\,\mathrm{byte}\)
\(1\,488\,\mathrm{byte}\)
\(1\,497\,\mathrm{byte}\)

explanation: Three label entries use \(3 \times  4 = 12\,\mathrm{byte}\). \(1\,500 - 12 = 1\,488\,\mathrm{byte}\) is still available for the original packet. It's the whole entry, not just the 20-bit label value that has to be counted.

prompt: A traffic engineering tunnel requires \(5\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\). The table shows three candidates with total route cost and minimum spare capacity along each path. Choose the lowest cost among the compliant paths.

options.text: None of the paths
Path B
Path A
Path C

explanation: A has the lowest cost, but only \(3\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\) available on bottleneck and is excluded. B and C meet the \(5\,\mathrm{Mbit/s}\) requirement; B has the lowest cost of them. This illustrates the shortest path under a capacity condition.

prompt: The main path is A–B–D–E. Before a failure, a fallback path B–C–D is ready. Link B–D fails, and the rest of these links work. How can local Fast Reroute continue the traffic?

options.text: A-B-C-D-E
A–B–D–E through the failing link
A–C–E without indicating these links
B must wait for each sender to create a new IP address.

explanation: B may lead traffic through the prepared route B–C–D and back to the main path at D. The point is local repair with prepared forwarding.

prompt: A PE sends a packet of outer tunnel label 80 and inner service label 25. The next core grid has a rule of switching the outer label 80 to 61. No other operation is done in this jump. Which stack goes out, top first?

options.text: 61 without internal label

explanation: Swap applies to the external label used by the kernel in this jump. The service label is retained so the stack becomes [61, 25]. This allows the core to transport traffic without processing each customer service.

prompt: In the L3VPN architecture of the lecture, all P-routes in the core must store all customers' VPN routes in order for the PE-routes to reach each other.

options.text: True
False

explanation: The core can be forwarded by means of the transport label and information on the supplier network. The VPN routes and the customer context are handled in the PE layer; they do not need to be located in all P panes.

prompt: What is a central function of the network interface, NIC, in an interconnection network?

options.text: To replace all network switch with one local route table.
Connecting the host's data transmission to the network, including through buffering and package management.
To determine the physical topology of the entire network alone.
To guarantee unrestricted reception without buffers or flow control.

explanation: NCI is the interface between the host and the network. The lecture shows, among other things, transmission engines, buffers and data entry.

prompt: What is right about credit based flow control?

options.text: Sender uses credits representing the available buffer space at the consignee's premises.
Sender can send without credit and only wait after the recipient has dropped the data.
The credit counts how many extra routing jumps a packet is allowed to take.
The consignor receives several credits for each consignment without the consignee releasing buffer space.

explanation: The sender may send when it has credit and reduce the credit when space is put into service. The receiver returns credit as space is released.

prompt: A network with lossless flow control automatically eliminates all possible errors, including bit errors and corrupted components.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Lossless flow control in this context prevents overflowing by stopping transmission before filling buffers. This concept does not imply that physical defects or other sources of error are impossible.

prompt: What concept determines which of the physical paths the packets can use?

options.text: Arbitration alone
Flow control alone
Route
Topology alone

explanation: The topology determines which paths exist physically. The route determines which of them are allowed or chosen. Arbitration determines who receives a resource when several competes.

prompt: What is the meaning of the Bible’s vision bandwidth in the lecture?

options.text: Average capacity along all possible pairs of paths.
The total capacity over a minimum cut that divides the end nodes into two equal groups.
The sum of the capacity of all links, regardless of the average they cross.
Maximum acceptance rate to one end node, regardless of topology.

explanation: Bissection examines a balanced section of the network. The capacity of the interconnections over the average tells us how much traffic can cross between halfs.

prompt: What is a direct interaction network as described in the lecture?

options.text: Calculation nodes are linked to the routes of the network topology itself, rather than to the leaves of a separate switch network only.
All nodes must be connected directly to all other nodes.
The calculation nodes must be aggregated at the leaves in a separate multi-level suite.
All messages must reach the destination without intermediate route jumps.

explanation: In the direct model, calculation nodes are linked to the routes through topology. In an indirect network, the calculation nodes are at the ends of a separate switch network. Direct does not necessarily mean completely connected.

prompt: Why should an Xoff message be sent before the recipient cache is full?

options.text: Xoff gives the sender several credits that must be used immediately.
Xoff requires the entire contents of the old buffer to be returned first.
All sent packets are automatically returned once at Xoff.
Data may already be on the way and continue to arrive before the sender has responded.

explanation: The stop message uses time until the sender is sent, and the data that has already been sent must still be received. The buffer therefore needs the safety clearance.

prompt: A basic multistage multistage topology may have internal conflicts even when two messages have different destinations.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Different end points don't guarantee that the internal paths are degraded. If traffic competes for the same internal link, one transfer may be blocked.

prompt: What is the difference between deadlock and livelock?

options.text: In deadlock only one link is full. Livelock requires delivery to the wrong node.
In deadlock, packets are stuck waiting on resource dependencies. In livelock, a packet can keep moving without reaching its destination.
In deadlock, packets keep moving without reaching their destination. In livelock, all affected packets are stuck waiting.
Deadlock is any short queue. Livelock is any retransmission after packet loss.

explanation: Deadlock results from blocked resource dependencies, often in a cycle. Livelock involves activity without completion, such as repeated rerouting that never reaches the destination.

prompt: Why can ordered use of dimensions in a mesh help to avoid deadlock?

options.text: It can remove cyclic channel dependencies by imposing a fixed resource usage order.
It makes all buffers infinite large.
It allows all packets to use all channels simultaneously.
It removes the need for physical connection between routers.

explanation: Dimension-order routing in the current mesh model arranges channel usage. Such a system can prevent circular waiting. The wraparound link network, like torus, requires further assessment.

prompt: What's the point of making a tree fat in a fat tree topology?

options.text: Making all cables physically thicker without changing capacity.
Using a single root link for all traffic, regardless of the number of nodes.
To place calculation nodes in all internal Switches as the only definition requirement.
To provide enough total capacity up in the tree to ensure that collapsing traffic is not automatically choked by narrow upper levels.

explanation: A regular tree can get little capacity near the root. Fat-tree builds more capacity towards upper tiers, e.g. with multiple interconnections, so that the Bisection capacity can be scaled up.

prompt: A crossbar can connect several pairs at the same time, but several consignors to the same exit may still have to compete for the exit.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Non-blocking does not mean infinite capacity into one receiver. The crossbar's simultaneous connections require that they do not require the same limited output at the same time.

prompt: Why can many-to-one traffic offer less efficient overall bandwidth than evenly distributed traffic?

options.text: All switched networks must then behave like an infinitely fast bus.
The capacity of the recipient or recipient link may become a bottleneck even if many consignors have available capacity.
The package payload automatically gets bigger for many senders.
Many senders do not need to be bitten anymore.

explanation: The integrated injection capacity is not sufficient. The traffic pattern may concentrate the load on a limited set of receivers, which therefore set a lower limit.

prompt: The fact that a Beneš topology is rearrangeably non-blocking means that new connections can always be established without changing any existing paths.

options.text: True
False

explanation: Rearrangeably means that a conflict-free connection can be found at reorganization. It may be necessary to change the paths already selected to accommodate the new combination.

prompt: A credit-controlled link sends at \(8\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\) using packets of \(100\,\mathrm{byte}\). The cable is \(100\,\mathrm{m}\) long, and signals travel at \(2 \times  10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}\). Assume the credit delay consists only of round-trip propagation, with no processing or other overhead. What is the minimum number of packet credits needed to keep the link busy?
explanation: A packet takes \(\frac{800\,\mathrm{bit}}{8\times10^9\,\mathrm{bit/s}}=0.1\,\mu\mathrm{s}\) to send. Round-trip propagation is \(\frac{2\times100}{2\times10^8}=1\,\mu\mathrm{s}\). The credit need is therefore \(\frac{1}{0.1} = 10\) packets. The simplified model omits other delays.

prompt: Xoff is sent when a buffer approaches fullness. After sending Xoff, data can still be found in \(5\,\mu\mathrm{s}\) with \(10\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\). Assume smooth bit current and no other delays. How much free buffer should be reserved for this data?

options.text: \(6\,250\,\mathrm{byte}\)
\(625\,\mathrm{byte}\)

explanation: The data still in flight after the stop signal is \(10 \times  10^{9}\,\mathrm{bit/s} \times  5 \times  10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s} = 50\,000\,\mathrm{bit}\). Dividing by 8 gives \(6\,250\,\mathrm{byte}\).

prompt: A packet on \(1\,000\,\mathrm{byte}\) is sent over a link on \(1\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\). So one-way propaganda is \(2\,\mu\mathrm{s}\). Ignore queue, routing and end-point work. What is the transport time from the shipment of the first bit to the last bit?

options.text: \(10\,\mu\mathrm{s}\)
\(2\,\mu\mathrm{s}\)
\(8\,\mu\mathrm{s}\)

explanation: Serialization takes \(\frac{8\,000\,\mathrm{bit}}{10^9\,\mathrm{bit/s}}=8\,\mu\mathrm{s}\). The last bit must also propagate for \(2\,\mu\mathrm{s}\). The total is \(8 + 2 = 10\,\mu\mathrm{s}\).

prompt: A basic 64 port multistage network is built with \(2\times 2\) suites. Use the \(\log_2 N\) step model and \(\frac{N}{2}\) switch at each step. How many total suites are used?
explanation: \(\log_2 64 = 6\) step. Each has \(\frac{64}{2} = 32\) suites. The total is \(6 \times  32 = 192\). This is the basic model, not the number of steps in a Beneš topology.

prompt: Compare an \(8\times 8\) mesh with a 6-dimensional hypercube, both with 64 nodes. Each link crossing the bisection offers \(10\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\) in each direction. Use the bisection counts of 8 and 32 in the table. What is the ratio of the hypercube’s one-way bisection bandwidth to the mesh’s?
explanation: The mesh has \(8 \times  10 = 80\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\) across the cut in one direction. The hypercube has \(32 \times  10 = 320\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\). Comparing the same direction gives a ratio of \(\frac{320}{80} = 4\).

prompt: A transmission sends repeat devices with \(900\,\mathrm{byte}\) payload and \(100\,\mathrm{byte}\) other data. Raw link speed is \(10\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\). Assume continuous transmission without other delays. What is the maximum payload flow?

options.text: \(1\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\)
\(0.9\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\)
\(9\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\)
\(10\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\)

explanation: The payload share is \(\frac{900}{900+100}=0.9\). This makes the payload flow \(10 \times  0.9 = 9\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\). Raw bandwidth also includes bits that are not the utility data of the application.

prompt: A build has two independent uplinks on \(100\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\) each. Assume that traffic can use both normally, and that the remaining link can take all traffic in case of one link error. What maximum overall traffic could the network have if full capacity is also to be maintained after such a failure?

options.text: \(200\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\)
\(150\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\)
\(400\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\)
\(100\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\)

explanation: Normally \(200\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\) is in total, but after one error only \(100\,\mathrm{Gbit/s}\) is left. The requirement to withstand the failure without capacity deficiency must be dimensioned according to this condition.

prompt: Two gateway routes, each with capacity for the whole load, are on the same circuit and are reached through each of their uplinks. The goal is to withstand the loss of one circuit. What action is best taken by the described weakness?

options.text: Give both gateways more memory, but keep common current.
Change the name of the wireless network.
Make sure that the gateways can be driven from independent power paths so that one circuit failure does not take both.
Increase the bandwidth of both uplinks without changing the power supply.

explanation: Two routers and two links do not protect against the common circuit. Independent flow paths remove the specified common error point; other sources of error have to be assessed separately.
source: Networking in the Real World · PDF pages 8, 11
